prompt: Draw on the metaphysics-of-emergence and virtual-reality literature to theorize how Aristotelian phantasia might illuminate the phenomenology of virtual perception.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis: Perception, Imagination, and the Grounds of Virtual Appearing Aristotle's account of phantasia is grounded in the prior operation of sense-perception, such that the image-making faculty cannot function independently of aisthesis; indeed, imagination is commonly held to be a kind of movement that cannot occur without sensation. Yet phantasia simultaneously contrasts with aisthesis, for it persists in the absence of the sensible object and thereby opens a domain of quasi-perceptual appearing irreducible to the immediate deliverances of the senses. Hawhee's reading of the *Rhetoric* underscores this interplay, noting that Aristotle inserts an explanatory remark clarifying phantasia's suasive force: "[I call things] in accordance with reason what people long for on the basis of persuasion; for they desire to see and possess many things after hearing about them" (Hawhee 2011, p. [PAGE NEEDED]). For in virtual environments, the user is similarly solicited into a mode of perceptual engagement that is not strictly sensory; the immersive environment "generates perceptual experience of the environment from a perspective within it, giving the user the sense of 'presence': that is, the sense of really being present at that perspective" (Chalmers, *The Virtual and the Real*, pp. 2–3). Accordingly, the distinction between phantasia and aisthesis maps productively onto the virtual–real distinction: the virtual percept, like the phantasma, arises through a movement occasioned by actual sensory stimulation yet operates in a register irreducible to it. Papachristou's insistence on leaving the term phantasia untranslated serves as a useful caution here, for "even though the Greek word 'phantasia' is usually translated it as 'imagination', I prefer to leave the word untranslated" (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). This terminological restraint preserves the concept's internal complexity—its grades from sensory to deliberative, its entanglement with doxa—which subsequent sections will explore. Burke, similarly, recognizes that imagination cannot be dismissed as merely psychological, noting that objections deeming such terms "overly psychologistic and extraliterary in its origins" are themselves dubious (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 97–99). Thus, the Aristotelian framework furnishes a vocabulary for describing how virtual perception constitutes a movement from actual sensation that nevertheless exceeds sensation's immediate scope. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia: The Image as Medium of Virtual Appearing If phantasia names the movement, then phantasma names its product—the quasi-perceptual content that persists after sensation ceases and through which the soul apprehends what is absent or not-yet-present. Heidegger's reading of *De Anima* is decisive on this point, for he insists that thinking itself cannot be severed from the phantasmatic: "If, however, even νοεῖν [the thorough deliberating of a matter, when I do not have it perceptually present] is something like a φαντασία or cannot be without φαντασία, then thinking too could not be without standing in the context of the entire life of a human being" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 149). The phantasma, accordingly, is not a mere by-product of perception but the indispensable medium through which deliberation, memory, and even noetic activity proceed. This medial function of the phantasma illuminates the virtual image with remarkable precision; virtual objects, as Ney reports of Chalmers's position, "really exist" and "virtual-world events really happen," such that "virtual-reality experiences are non-illusory" (Ney, *On Phenomenal Functionalism about the Properties of Virtual and Non-virtual Objects*, pp. 8–10). The phantasma thus occupies a structural position analogous to the virtual image: both are real without being identical to the sensory original, both sustain cognitive and affective engagement in the absence of their material referent. Burke's insight that imagination mediates between reason and appetite—serving to "recommend the dictates of reason to imagination, in order to excite the appetite and will" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96)—further clarifies how the phantasma is not passive but actively structures desire. The distinction between sensory and deliberative phantasia, which Papachristou traces across the grades of the faculty (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 6–7), signals that the phantasma produced at each level differs qualitatively; the full taxonomy of these grades will be elaborated in subsequent chapters. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mneme: Memory, Persistence, and the Temporality of Virtual Experience The relationship between phantasia and memory discloses a further dimension of the virtual, for Aristotle holds that memory is a state or affection of perception conditioned by the lapse of time and directed exclusively at the past. The phantasma in memory bears a dual character—it is at once an object of contemplation in itself, a theorema, and a likeness of the thing remembered, an eikon. Heidegger's emphasis on the embeddedness of thought in the whole life of the human being (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 149) suggests that memory's phantasmata are never isolated mental contents but rather movements situated within a broader existential context—a context that virtual reality both simulates and transforms. Burke's recognition that apprehension alters the will (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96) implies that the mnemonic phantasma carries an affective charge capable of reshaping practical orientation; in virtual environments, the persistence of such images after the headset is removed testifies to phantasia's residual kinetic power. O'Gorman reinforces this connection between phantasia and the appearing function of discourse, noting that Aristotle associates lexis with phantasia, "saying of lexis, 'but all these things are forms of outward show [phantasia] and intended to affect the audience'" (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). The voluntariness of phantasia at this mnemonic level—whether one can summon or dismiss the remembered image at will—remains a contested question whose full treatment is deferred to the chapter on habituated phantasia. 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa: Belief, Judgment, and the Epistemic Status of Virtual Objects Aristotle distinguishes phantasia from doxa insofar as phantasia can be true or false yet does not entail the commitment characteristic of belief; one may entertain a phantasma of something fearful without judging that the feared object is present. This distinction proves indispensable for theorizing the epistemic status of virtual perception, for the virtual perceiver inhabits a space in which the appearing of objects solicits engagement without necessarily compelling belief in their non-virtual existence. Heidegger's reading of rhetoric illuminates this point, for rhetoric has its sight on "κρίσις, view-construction, a definite decision in the sense of a δόξα" and that the speaker must bring the audience "into a corresponding frame of mind" through discourse itself (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 124). The virtual environment, analogously, constructs a perceptual κρίσις—a scene of judgment—within which the user must decide whether and how to credit the appearing image. Chalmers's virtual realism, which holds that virtual objects possess genuine properties and that experiences in virtual reality need not be illusory (Chalmers, *The Virtual and the Real*, pp. 1–2), pushes the phantasia–doxa distinction toward a new articulation: if virtual objects are real, then the phantasia they occasion may be veridical rather than merely apparent. Yet the tension between phantasia's causal derivation from sensation and its functional autonomy in deliberation and dreaming complicates any simple alignment. Papachristou's tripartite schema of grades of phantasia (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 6–7) suggests that at the deliberative level, phantasia interacts with doxa in ways that the sensory grade does not; accordingly, the full elaboration of how belief modulates virtual phantasia—and whether habituated engagement with virtual environments reshapes the faculty itself—will be pursued in the dedicated sections on deliberative phantasia and habituated phantasia that follow.
